To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a deep learning model trained on LIDCs IDRI dataset performs comparably with humans on an independent dataset with histopathological groundtruth.
A system trained on the LIDC dataset, performs comparably to humans on an independent dataset of nodules with histopathological confirmation of malignancy.

a deep learning model trained on a large public dataset can predict the malignancy risk in two datasets from an independent lung screening trial with performance similar to that of human readers and better than that of a clinical model.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question whether a deep learning system trained on the LIDC/IDRI dataset is useful to support clinical decision making.
the evaluation of a system trained on LIDCD IDRI data on independent data.
the performance evaluation of a deep learning model on an external dataset with histopathological ground-truth and comparison of this model with a set of human observers and the clinical model.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

deep learning systems can be trained to predict the malignancy risk with a performance that is comparable to humans and the clinical model, but more research is needed on the performance in different datasets and the clinical impact of the models.
deep learning systems have the potential to outperform humans and clinical models, but the performance of deep learning systems on independent data is highly dependent on the data and the model.
a deep learning system performs comparably with humans in predicting malignancy risk in a subset of lung nodules, but the performance of the deep learning system is dependent on the dataset used.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
deep learning is an interesting approach that is able to predict the malignancy risk in nodules, but it is not yet mature enough to be used as a standalone diagnostic system.
the system performs well on one dataset but not as well on the other, and that the system does not perform as well in the dataset where the human readers also perform poorly.

the system performs better than a clinical model and comparabily with humans in one dataset, while it performs comparabily with a clinical model and worse than humans in another dataset, which suggests that the system may benefit from further training on a larger, more diverse dataset.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the deep learning system is able to perform as well as human observers in one dataset but not in the other.
a system trained on LIDCD IDRI data performs well on an independent dataset with a solid ground truth.
a deep learning model, trained on LINC IDRI, performs well on an external dataset, and that a deep learning system can be a viable alternative to human readers for lung cancer screening.
